title: Primary Myelofibrosis: Development of a Personalized Medicine
content: Background/Objectives: Primary myelofibrosis (PMF) is a myeloproliferative neoplasm, associated with a somatic mutation in the JAK2, CALR, MPL genes and characterized by progressive bone marrow fibrosis, extramedullary hematopoiesis, splenomegaly, constitutional symptoms, progressive cytopenias, and in a subset of patients, leukemic transformation. The aim of the present study is to review recent studies investigating molecular abnormalities observed in myelofibrosis and showing how these studies have led to the development of new therapeutic strategies for PMF. Methods: An extensive search of the most recent literature was performed, selecting and critically analyzing the most relevant studies. Results: The studies carried out in the last years have provided an extensive molecular characterization of PMF, showing its heterogeneity, characterized by the presence of additional cytogenetic and non-driver gene mutations that contribute to disease evolution. The molecular abnormalities, together with clinical parameters, provided criteria for a risk score stratification of PMF patients. The molecular characterization of PMF has triggered the development of targeted therapeutics represented by JAK inhibitors and antibodies targeting mutant CALR. Conclusions: PMF is a complex and heterogeneous disease that needs to be carefully characterized at molecular and clinical level at diagnosis, to provide a careful risk stratification of individual patients and an adequate personalized treatment.
